extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and humor theory; readers of Kant's Critique of Judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Immanuel Kant's §54 account of laughter: the incongruity-as-nothing theory that specifies conditions under which a stimulus is comic. Useful for analyzing jokes, comic situations, and distinctions between humor and other affects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining formula
rubrics_metrics.description: "Laughter is an affection arising from the sudden transformation of a strained expectation into nothing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This canonical sentence is the compact statement of the theory; use it as the primary test when judging whether an event qualifies as laughter-worthy. All further criteria (strained expectation, suddenness, transformation into nothing, bodily resonance) are unpackings of this formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strained expectation (gespannte Erwartung)
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke or comic situation must first build up a particular cognitive anticipation: a definite, specific expectation in the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a setup that creates a clear expectation, there is no 'payoff' for the reduction-to-nothing. Evaluate whether the stimulus produces a concrete, testable expectation rather than merely a vague mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suddenness (plötzlich)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dissolution of the expectation must occur in an instant; the change must be abrupt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow disambiguation or gradual reinterpretation does not produce the bodily affect of laughter. If the audience has time to form an alternative cognition, the affect will be understanding/appreciation rather than laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation into nothing (in nichts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation must not be transformed into the opposite or into a significant new truth; it must be shown to be void—reduced to insignificance or nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is decisive for distinguishing humor from disappointment (expectation → painful opposite) and from insight (expectation → meaningful new cognition). Good comic payoff renders the prior anticipation unsatisfied in a way that leaves no new content for the understanding to rest on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily resonance (physical pleasure)
rubrics_metrics.description: The play of mental representations triggers a play of the bodily organs (diaphragm, lungs); the pleasure involved is physical rather than purely intellectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the pleasurable response is experienced as bodily release rather than as purely cognitive satisfaction. Kant emphasizes an oscillation that 'spills over' into bodily movement (laughter), not mere intellectual insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setup must create a definite, testable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial material must specify an expectation that can be checked by the subsequent event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a joke, identify the specific expectation the audience is led to form. Vague or purely associative setups fail this test and are less likely to produce Kantian laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punchline must show expectation to be void (not merely wrong)
rubrics_metrics.description: The humorous resolution must reveal the expectation to be void—neither confirmed nor replaced by an intelligible opposite, but exposed as insignificant or nonsensical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: a punchline that simply inverts the expectation (leading to disappointment or irony) or that supplies an explanatory insight (leading to appreciation) rather than voiding it. Examples from Kant: the empty beer bottle, the paid mourners doing 'less and less the more I pay them', the Indian's puzzlement about how beer 'got into' the bottle—each collapses the expectational explanation into nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief mental vacuum—the understanding finds no satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a short interval in which the understanding cannot rest in any new cognition; this vacancy is essential to the ensuing bodily pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the audience experiences a momentary lack of cognitive completion before the bodily response. If the mind immediately substitutes a new coherent cognition, laughter per Kant is unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure derives from oscillation, not content of either side
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure of laughter comes from the oscillation between expectation and its reduction to nothing, not from the truth, beauty, or intrinsic interest of either the setup or the resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish pleasures that come from content (e.g., admiration at marvels, appreciation of beauty, intellectual insight) from the bodily play that Kant attributes to comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude things that please by truth or beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Items that please by their truth or beauty are aesthetic pleasures but are not comic according to Kant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying a stimulus as comic, rule out cases where the pleasure is due to recognition of truth, beauty, or cognitive gain; such pleasures belong to aesthetics or understanding, not to laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude mere astonishment at marvels (admiration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere astonishment or wonder at marvels produces admiration, not the comic affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the affect is dominated by awe or amazement rather than the bodily play of laughter, it fails Kant's criteria for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude painful surprises (shocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprises that produce pain are shocks, not laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that elicit fear, pain, or distress—even if they disrupt expectation—are not comic in Kant's sense. Check affective valence: is it pleasurable bodily play or painful alarm?

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude slow-revealed truths (understanding, not wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revelations that unfold slowly and result in understanding are intellectual gains, not instances of wit that produce laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the resolution supplies a new cognition that satisfies the understanding over time, categorize it as intellectual insight rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic checklist (practical test questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four questions to diagnose Kantian humor: Does the setup create a definite, testable expectation? Does the punchline dissolve that expectation into nothing (not into the opposite)? Is there a brief mental vacuum in which the understanding finds no satisfaction? Is the pleasure felt as bodily release rather than as intellectual gain?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these yes/no questions as a quick heuristic when analyzing a comic stimulus. A 'yes' to all makes the stimulus a good candidate for Kantian laughter.
